items.section: 3.7 Structural-protein surface — a matrix as a living set: a self
items.text: Individual vault particles lower their height under an imaging force and return it when that force lowers. The particles are rat major vault protein expressed in HighFive insect cells from a recombinant baculovirus, sucrose-gradient purified, adsorbed on a highly ordered pyrolytic graphite surface in TMS buffer and imaged in liquid by atomic force microscopy in jumping mode, with rectangular silicon-nitride cantilevers of nominal spring constant 0.05 N/m calibrated by Sader's method. Mean heights are 38 ± 2 nm for particles reclining on the barrel and 35.5 ± 2 nm for half particles adsorbed at the waist, against 40 nm and 33.5 nm from X-ray. Across sequential topographies at approximately 3 min intervals with the imaging force altered frame to frame, one half particle's height drops abruptly from 36 nm to 15 nm and returns to its original height at lower imaging force, and 15 nm matches the size of a cap alone. The strain is approximately 60% at half particles and approximately 10% at reclining particles, and the half-particle result repeats at further particles. One reclining particle loses height across the frames with partial returns at frames 4, 7 and 10, and a comparison of frames 1 and 7 carries partial collapse at the barrel. Stiffness and breaking force are 0.03 ± 0.01 N/m and 122 ± 83 pN across 13 reclining particles and 0.06 ± 0.03 N/m and 165 ± 38 pN across 21 half particles, from 21 and 120 indentation curves. A half particle imaged across 37 frames at a held 65 pN breaks first at the barrel, the cap tilting and the particle losing its axial symmetry.

items.section: 3.7 Structural-protein surface — a matrix as a living set: a self
items.text: Fractures induced at the barrel of individual vault particles by an atomic force microscope tip close again over time while the particle stands in a liquid environment at room temperature, and the fractures run along the contacts between two neighbouring major vault proteins, in the direction those proteins align. Recovery times part into three: a restoration of force during the backward curve, under 650 ms; no restoration of force with the next topography carrying an intact particle, 650 ms to 2 s; and the fractured topography imaged whole before its recovery, over 2 s. Across 617 force-indentation curves at 26 half particles and 28 reclining particles, 179 of 260 curves at half particles, 70%, recover under 650 ms, against 22% at reclining particles. Twenty-two events of reversible topographic damage stand at 11 different reclining particles, each over 2 s, registered by switching off the y-scan and enabling only the x-scan. One reclining particle returns to its first shape within 90 s, the time to take one complete image. The average energy supplied across a breakage-and-recovery cycle is 220 ± 34 kBT at reclining particles and 302 ± 34 kBT at half particles. Single steps at the indentation curves are 1.3 ± 0.95 nm and 117 ± 50 pN, approximately 20 kBT each, against 2 kBT at a hydrophobic interaction and 8 kBT at a hydrogen bond. The strongest major-vault-protein contacts stand between cap-helix domains, 29 of the 41 residue pairs at that interface hydrophobic, against 16 hydrogen bonds, 5 ionic bonds and 10 hydrophobic contacts at the barrel, a bonding energy between two alpha-helices approximately four times that between two beta-sheet domains; fractures were detected at the barrel surface only.
